professionalScope.en: Continuing professional education for licensed clinicians and allied providers. Every learner gets the same evidence, regulatory status and safety content; what each may do with it — prescribe, recommend, administer, or refer — follows their own licence and scope, and the course adapts its practice guidance to that role. It informs clinical reasoning; it is not a protocol, contains no dosing, and does not replace specialist input, formal guidelines or individual judgment.

disclaimers.en: Educational content for clinicians. It does not prescribe, and it never restates an evidence grade above what the source assigns to the specific indication.
Regulatory statements name their jurisdiction. US compounding examples (FDA 503A/503B) do not describe UK or EU status.
Designed toward future CME accreditation. No CME or CE credit is currently offered.

claims.text: The skin works as a peripheral neuro-immuno-endocrine organ: reviews describe four immuno-endocrine units (epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, adnexal) whose cells make and respond to hormones and signal to neighbouring cells, through sensory nerves, and through the circulation. This is a mechanistic framework drawn from cell, tissue and animal work.

refs.title: Neuro-immuno-endocrinology of the skin: how environment regulates body homeostasis
Neuroendocrinology of the skin
The human skin as a hormone target and an endocrine gland
Neuronal control of skin function: the skin as a neuroimmunoendocrine organ
Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology — A Clinician's Pocket Guide

claims.text: Skin cells carry the enzymes to make steroids from cholesterol (CYP11A1) and to activate circulating precursors (11β-HSD1, 5α-reductase, aromatase), producing cortisol, DHT and estradiol locally; this rests mainly on cell, tissue and biochemical studies.

refs.title: Steroidogenesis in the skin: implications for local immune functions
The human skin as a hormone target and an endocrine gland
Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology — A Clinician's Pocket Guide

claims.text: Human scalp hair follicles kept in organ culture respond to CRH by making POMC products, secrete cortisol, and switch off their own CRH in response to glucocorticoid — an HPA-like loop running without systemic connections (human tissue, ex vivo).

refs.title: Human hair follicles display a functional equivalent of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and synthesize cortisol

claims.text: In mice, deleting glucocorticoid synthesis in keratinocytes causes spontaneous skin inflammation and worse experimental dermatitis: keratinocyte-made glucocorticoids set local immune tone (animal evidence, with a human association with inflammatory skin disease).

refs.title: Keratinocytes control skin immune homeostasis through de novo-synthesized glucocorticoids

claims.text: The skin also runs shortened thyroid-like (TRH, TSH, deiodinase-generated T3) and somatotropic (GH/IGF-1) loops; the thyroid-like evidence comes mainly from mouse models and the follicle GH/IGF-1 loop from human follicles ex vivo.

refs.title: Thyroid hormone action in epidermal development and homeostasis and its implications in the pathophysiology of the skin
Human Hair Follicles Operate a Functional Peripheral Equivalent of the Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Somatotropic Axis Ex Vivo
Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology — A Clinician's Pocket Guide

claims.text: The skin supplies a whole-body hormone system: UVB converts 7-dehydrocholesterol to previtamin D3 in human skin, and vitamin D3 is carried into the circulation to be hydroxylated to 25(OH)D and then calcitriol (skin-to-body signalling).

refs.title: Photosynthesis of previtamin D3 in human skin and the physiologic consequences
Vitamin D metabolism, mechanism of action, and clinical applications
Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology — A Clinician's Pocket Guide

claims.text: Reviews describe a skin contribution to circulating androgens and estrogens, especially in older people — a second skin-to-body route, supported mainly by biochemical data.

refs.title: Steroidogenesis in the skin: implications for local immune functions
The human skin as a hormone target and an endocrine gland

claims.text: Systemic hormones act on skin (body-to-skin): cortisol excess thins the dermis and causes striae and bruising; hypothyroidism gives dry, coarse skin and myxoedema. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide treats the aesthetic exam as a systemic screen and lists suspected Cushing syndrome (violaceous striae, central obesity, proximal weakness, new hypertension or diabetes) and rapidly progressive virilisation among reasons to refer promptly to endocrinology.

refs.title: Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology — A Clinician's Pocket Guide
Thyroid hormone action on skin

claims.text: The Hormone Cell Atlas (Science 2026) analysed RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in about 14 million single cells and nuclei from 47 human tissues, skin among them, and mapped putative hormone-producing and hormone-receiving cell types.

refs.title: A Hormone Cell Atlas maps the human endocrine system at cellular resolution
Hormone Cell Atlas portal — About and FAQs

claims.text: The atlas's authors describe its scores as putative and hypothesis-generating, not functional hormones and receptors, and leave validation to in vitro and in vivo work; more generally, transcript levels alone often fail to predict protein levels. A transcriptomic map therefore shows capacity, not secretion or effect.

refs.title: Hormone Cell Atlas portal — About and FAQs
A Hormone Cell Atlas maps the human endocrine system at cellular resolution
On the Dependency of Cellular Protein Levels on mRNA Abundance
Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology — A Clinician's Pocket Guide

claims.text: The guide infers from the atlas that the skin, built from every major cell lineage, is plausibly one of the body's largest distributed endocrine signalling networks — an inference from transcriptomic prediction, not a measurement.

refs.title: Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology — A Clinician's Pocket Guide
A Hormone Cell Atlas maps the human endocrine system at cellular resolution

claims.text: Topical and transdermal treatments act through receptors the skin already carries, and local steroid-metabolising enzymes modify potency, so the cutaneous response need not mirror the dose; receptor presence is a hypothesis-generating starting point that needs validation, and says nothing yet about efficacy in people.

refs.title: Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology — A Clinician's Pocket Guide
Hormone Cell Atlas portal — About and FAQs

claims.text: The guide's testing pearl says serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D falls with sunscreen use; an independent systematic review found that sunscreen blocks vitamin D synthesis under artificial UV, but randomized field trials of daily moderate-SPF sunscreen did not lower 25(OH)D, and high-SPF products have not been trialled.

refs.title: The effect of sunscreen on vitamin D: a review
Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology — A Clinician's Pocket Guide

claims.text: Senescent cells are permanently growth-arrested yet still secreting; the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (IL-6, IL-8, matrix metalloproteinases, growth factors) was characterised in cultured human cells after DNA damage.

refs.title: Senescence-associated secretory phenotypes reveal cell-nonautonomous functions of oncogenic RAS and the p53 tumor suppressor
Faces of cellular senescence in skin aging
Biomarkers of Cellular Senescence and Skin Aging

claims.text: In human skin, cells carrying the senescence marker p16INK4a are more numerous with age in both epidermis and dermis; no single universal marker identifies senescent cells, so counts depend on the marker used.

refs.title: p16INK4A is a robust in vivo biomarker of cellular aging in human skin
Biomarkers of Cellular Senescence and Skin Aging
Faces of cellular senescence in skin aging

claims.text: In 178 adults of the Leiden Longevity Study, more p16-positive cells in sun-protected arm skin were associated with ageing-type elastic fibres, more facial wrinkles and higher perceived age independent of chronological age; people in the lowest tertile of epidermal p16 counts looked about 3 years younger than those in the highest. This is an association, not evidence of cause.

refs.title: P16INK4a Positive Cells in Human Skin Are Indicative of Local Elastic Fiber Morphology, Facial Wrinkling, and Perceived Age
refs.publication: J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci · 2016;71:1022–1028

claims.text: Skin collagen falls with age; aged human dermis shows more fibroblast MMP-1, fragmented collagen and fibroblasts under less mechanical tension that make less procollagen, and culture work shows fragmentation feeds back to raise MMP-1. That senescent cells drive this in living skin is plausible but not shown.

refs.title: The influence of age and sex on skin thickness, skin collagen and density
Decreased collagen production in chronologically aged skin: roles of age-dependent alteration in fibroblast function and defective mechanical stimulation
Collagen fragmentation promotes oxidative stress and elevates matrix metalloproteinase-1 in fibroblasts in aged human skin

claims.text: Causal evidence that senescent cells drive ageing comes from mice: clearing p16-positive cells extended healthy lifespan and senolytics improved function and survival in old mice; skin was checked only for safety (thickness, fibrosis, wound closure), and clearing p16-positive cells during healing slowed wound closure.

refs.title: Naturally occurring p16(Ink4a)-positive cells shorten healthy lifespan
Senolytics improve physical function and increase lifespan in old age

claims.text: Human senotherapy data are small pilots with tissue-marker endpoints — an open-label senolytic pilot in 9 patients reduced epidermal p16/p21-positive cells; an exploratory topical rapamycin RCT (36 enrolled, 19 lost) reduced skin p16 — clinical improvement in that trial was described only in 'multiple participants', and no adequately sized trial with clinical skin-ageing outcomes was found on PubMed or ClinicalTrials.gov (checked 24 September 2026). The guide advises that senolytics generally be confined to clinical trials.

Targeting cellular senescence in dermatology: senolytic and senomorphic strategies

claims.text: Interventions on the ageing matrix with human trials: daily sunscreen slowed photoageing in a 903-person community RCT (B); topical tretinoin improves photoageing consistently across randomized trials and the guide rates topical retinoids first-line GRADE A; topical retinol improved fine wrinkles in very old skin in a small RCT (C), and within a week lowered MMPs and raised collagen synthesis in aged human skin.

claims.text: The skin expresses the elements of a local HPA-like axis (CRH, POMC, ACTH) and regenerates active cortisol from cortisone through 11β-HSD1 in keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts; 11β-HSD1 activity is higher in aged and photo-exposed human skin, local glucocorticoid availability is regulated independently of circulating levels, and 11β-HSD1 knockout mice are protected from age-induced dermal atrophy.

claims.text: The only human RCT of 11β-HSD1 inhibition with skin outcomes is a 28-person pilot in type 2 diabetes: it missed its primary outcome (skin 11β-HSD1 activity), showed an exploratory reduction in wound size, and modestly impaired barrier function. No registered trial tests an 11β-HSD1 inhibitor for skin ageing, and the compound tested has no FDA approval (ClinicalTrials.gov and Drugs@FDA checked 24 Sep 2026).

claims.text: Per the Endocrine Society diagnostic guideline, the features that best discriminate Cushing's syndrome are easy bruising, facial plethora, proximal myopathy and striae that are reddish-purple and wider than 1 cm; facial fullness, dorsocervical fat pad, weight gain, acne, hirsutism, thin skin and fatigue are common in the general population and less discriminatory.

refs.title: The diagnosis of Cushing's syndrome: an Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline
Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology — A Clinician's Pocket Guide

claims.text: Endogenous Cushing's syndrome is uncommon (2–3 new cases per million per year in European population studies); the commonest cause of Cushing's syndrome is iatrogenic, and the guideline recommends a drug history (oral, inhaled, topical, injected — including skin-bleaching creams, herbal tonics and joint or nerve injections) before any biochemical testing.

refs.title: The diagnosis of Cushing's syndrome: an Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline

claims.text: The guideline recommends testing patients with multiple and progressive features (particularly the discriminating ones) or features unusual for age, recommends against widespread testing and against random serum cortisol, and sends abnormal results to an endocrinologist. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide adds that consumer cortisol panels are poorly validated and reads most popular 'cortisol face' as a lifestyle-and-fluid picture.

refs.title: The diagnosis of Cushing's syndrome: an Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline
Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology — A Clinician's Pocket Guide

claims.text: Human skin expresses ERα, ERβ and GPR30 in aged and photoaged sites; two weeks of topical estradiol raised procollagen I/III in sun-protected hip skin of postmenopausal women but not in photoaged forearm or facial skin.

refs.title: Induction of collagen by estradiol: difference between sun-protected and photodamaged human skin in vivo
Estrogens and aging skin

claims.text: In small observational biopsy studies, skin collagen content and thickness fall by about 1–2% per year after menopause, in step with bone mass, tracking years since menopause more than chronological age. The 'up to 30% in the first five years' figure quoted by reviews and by the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide is not stated in the primary abstracts it traces to; the lesson reports it as a review figure.

claims.text: Small RCTs of systemic hormone therapy increased skin thickness (n=60, 12 months) and skin collagen (n=41, 6 months) at non-facial sites; a 2023 meta-analysis pooling small, heterogeneous studies (some non-randomized) reports higher elasticity, thickness and collagen, and its authors do not propose MHT as an independent treatment for skin ageing.

claims.text: The largest RCT of hormone therapy on facial skin (485 women, 48 weeks, low-dose) found no significant difference from placebo in wrinkling or sagging, and a 4-year randomized study in recently menopausal women (KEEPS) found no difference in wrinkle or rigidity scores. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide grades the skin benefit B; the NAMS 2022 statement rates its skin key point Level II (limited or inconsistent); the course grades the structural effects C and states that a visible wrinkle benefit has not been shown in the largest trials.

claims.text: Topical estrogen: a 24-week RCT (n=54) of a conjugated-estrogen cream improved facial skin thickness and fine wrinkles versus placebo cream, and a small randomized study found topical estrogen accelerated acute wound healing in healthy older adults. In the US an OTC product promoted as a hormone cream is regarded as an unapproved new drug (21 CFR 310.530), and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide advises against off-label estrogen for wrinkles (GRADE C).

claims.text: In the US (FDA request of 10 Nov 2025; first approved labels 12 Feb 2026), approved uses of menopausal hormone therapy are moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms, vulvovaginal/genitourinary symptoms and, for some products, prevention of bone loss; the labeling changes removed cardiovascular, breast-cancer and probable-dementia statements from the boxed warning and did not add skin as an indication.

claims.text: The NAMS 2022 position statement finds the benefit–risk ratio favourable for bothersome VMS and prevention of bone loss in women under 60 or within 10 years of menopause without contraindications, and finds insufficient evidence and safety concerns for compounded bioidentical hormone therapy (patient preference alone should not justify it); WHI findings do not support MHT for chronic disease prevention. Skin benefit is secondary and never on its own an indication (Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide).

claims.text: Low-dose vaginal estrogen is effective for moderate-to-severe genitourinary syndrome of menopause without an added progestogen — the one setting where estrogen is given for the tissue itself.

refs.title: The 2020 genitourinary syndrome of menopause position statement of The North American Menopause Society

claims.text: Skin-directed care with stronger evidence: daily broad-spectrum sunscreen reduced measured skin ageing over 4.5 years in a 903-person independent RCT, and in the US one tretinoin cream is FDA-approved as an adjunct for mitigating fine facial wrinkles (its label states it does not eliminate wrinkles or reverse photoaging).

claims.text: In a consecutive NIH series of 32 people with MEN1, 88% had multiple facial angiofibromas (identical to those of tuberous sclerosis) and 72% collagenomas; angiofibromas outside tuberous sclerosis warrant biochemical testing for MEN1.

refs.title: Multiple facial angiofibromas and collagenomas in patients with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1
Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology — A Clinician's Pocket Guide

claims.text: Carney complex (over 70% carry inactivating PRKAR1A variants) presents with lentigines typically on the face, lips and mucosa (canthal pigmentation is seen only in Carney complex and Peutz–Jeghers syndrome), blue naevi and cutaneous myxomas (eyelid, ear, nipple); cardiac myxomas occur in 20–40% and cause more than half of disease mortality, which is why early detection and echocardiographic screening matter.

claims.text: In MEN2A, cutaneous lichen amyloidosis — most often over the scapular upper back — clusters with RET codon-634 variants and is typically detected before medullary thyroid cancer.

refs.title: Thyroid Malignancy and Cutaneous Lichen Amyloidosis: Key Points Amid RET Pathogenic Variants in Medullary Thyroid Cancer/Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 2 (MEN2)
Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology — A Clinician's Pocket Guide

claims.text: Primary adrenal insufficiency causes hyperpigmentation particularly of sun-exposed areas, skin creases, mucosa and scars; the Endocrine Society recommends testing acutely ill patients with such signs and treating a suspected adrenal crisis before test results are available.

refs.title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Primary Adrenal Insufficiency: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline

claims.text: A rapid pace or progression of hirsutism, or virilization (clitoromegaly, deepening voice, increasing muscularity), points to a greater likelihood of an androgen-secreting neoplasm (about 0.2% of hyperandrogenic women; over half malignant); the Endocrine Society suggests against androgen testing in women with regular cycles and unwanted local hair without an abnormal hirsutism score.

claims.text: Other common endocrine skin signs: acanthosis nigricans tracks hyperinsulinaemia and insulin resistance; pretibial myxoedema reflects thyrotropin-receptor stimulation in Graves' disease; cold, dry skin suggests hypothyroidism.

claims.text: Dermal white adipose tissue is a distinct adipocyte layer in the reticular dermis. In mice it expands after Staphylococcus aureus infection and its adipocytes release cathelicidin, and this antimicrobial capacity declines with age through TGF-β signalling. In human skin the layer is arranged in cones around pilosebaceous units, and human acne lesions contain perifollicular preadipocytes that express cathelicidin; its contribution to human skin ageing has not been measured.

claims.text: The subcutaneous fat of the face is partitioned into discrete anatomical compartments, and facial ageing is in part how these compartments change.

refs.title: The fat compartments of the face: anatomy and clinical implications for cosmetic surgery
Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology — A Clinician's Pocket Guide

claims.text: In 186 pairs of identical twins, a four-point higher BMI was associated with an older appearance before about age 40 and a younger appearance after 40.

refs.title: Factors contributing to the facial aging of identical twins

claims.text: Glycation proceeds non-enzymatically from Schiff base to Amadori product to advanced glycation end products (AGEs); AGEs cross-link long-lived collagen and, through RAGE, activate inflammatory signalling in laboratory and animal studies. A&RE rates the structural and inflammatory claims GRADE B; the course grades the causal link to visible skin ageing D because the human evidence is associative.

claims.text: In human skin biopsies, collagen glycoxidation products (CML, pentosidine) and collagen fluorescence rise about five-fold between ages 20 and 85 and are up to twice as high in type 1 diabetes; human skin collagen has an estimated half-life of about 15 years.

refs.title: Accumulation of Maillard reaction products in skin collagen in diabetes and aging

claims.text: Skin autofluorescence correlates moderately (r = 0.47–0.62) with skin-biopsy AGE measures and was validated in non-pigmented skin; it is a surrogate reading of AGE load.

refs.title: Simple non-invasive assessment of advanced glycation endproduct accumulation

claims.text: Products sold as 'anti-glycation' are tested on surrogate readings or appearance scores; A&RE rates them GRADE C on surrogate endpoints, and no trial found for this course measured collagen cross-links in human skin.

refs.title: Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology — A Clinician's Pocket Guide

claims.text: GLP-1 and GIP are incretins that amplify glucose-dependent insulin secretion; GLP-1 also slows gastric emptying and reduces food intake, and native GLP-1 is degraded within minutes. Semaglutide is a long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonist; tirzepatide is a dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist.

claims.text: Across 35 randomized trials of incretin drugs, a median of about 28% (IQR 16–40%) of the weight lost was muscle-related tissue, and no trial reported objective physical function; the US labels state that fat mass loss exceeds lean mass loss.

claims.text: Human evidence on facial change during incretin-driven weight loss is observational and small: a retrospective imaging study of 20 patients found a median 9% loss of midface volume, mostly superficial and about 7% per 10 kg lost, and a survey of 1,226 patients found self-reported sagging, facial volume loss and hair loss rising with the percentage of weight lost. units.title: The skin as an endocrine organ, and how it ages · three lessons

blocks.title: The skin makes its own hormones.
blocks.narration: This course starts with physiology, because every later question about a hormone or peptide for skin rests on it. Skin senses hormones from the blood, makes several of its own, and ages in ways that change both. In three lessons you will separate what happens locally in the skin from what the rest of the body sends in, and label each finding by the kind of evidence behind it.
blocks.sourceNote: Hormones and Peptides for Skin · Module 01 · course opener

blocks.title: How will you use this course?
blocks.narration: The evidence, grades and regulatory facts are the same for everyone. What changes, in every module, is the 'what you do next' at the end of each lesson, so it fits what your licence lets you do.
blocks.sourceNote: Audience decision, Omar Saleem 2026-09-22 · course-wide role router

blocks.title: Four units, one circuit.
blocks.narration: Think of the skin as a sensing organ with its own hormone supply. Researchers who study it describe four units, epidermal, dermal, hypodermal and adnexal, the last meaning hair follicles and glands. Each unit holds cells that can make hormones and mount an immune response, such as keratinocytes, fibroblasts, sebocytes, fat cells and mast cells. Signals move three ways. Neighbouring cells talk directly, sensory nerves carry messages in and out, and some products enter the blood and reach distant organs. Keep one distinction in view for the whole module. A signal that is made and used inside the skin is a local loop. A hormone that arrives from the blood, or leaves the skin for the rest of the body, is systemic signalling. Much of what follows is mechanism, drawn from cell, tissue and animal studies, and each finding will be labelled that way.
blocks.sourceNote: Slominski 2025 · Slominski & Wortsman 2000 · Zouboulis 2004 · Roosterman 2006 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 5–6

blocks.title: A steroid factory with local axes.
blocks.narration: Skin cells carry the enzymes to build steroids from cholesterol or to activate precursors arriving in the blood, and they run shortened copies of the body's central hormone axes. Each row names the evidence it rests on, because most of it comes from cells, tissue kept alive outside the body, or mice.
blocks.sourceNote: Slominski 2013 · Ito 2005 · Phan 2021 · Mancino 2021 · Horesh 2023 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 6

blocks.title: Three directions of traffic.
blocks.narration: Hormone signals in skin run in three directions. Some are made and used in the same patch of skin. Some arrive from the blood. A few leave the skin and act on the rest of the body. Knowing which one you are looking at decides whether the answer lies in the skin or in a systemic assessment.
blocks.sourceNote: Slominski 2025 · Phan 2021 · Ito 2005 · Holick 1980 · Bikle 2014 · Safer 2011 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 5–7

blocks.title: Read the skin before the serum.
blocks.narration: Picture the consultation where a patient asks about thinning, bruising skin. The Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide asks you to read that skin as a window on the whole endocrine system before reaching for a serum. Sudden thinning with easy bruising suggests cortisol excess. Coarse, dry, cool skin suggests an underactive thyroid. New acanthosis nigricans points to insulin resistance. The guide lists violaceous striae with new hypertension or diabetes, rapidly progressive virilisation, and signs of an endocrine tumour as reasons to refer promptly to endocrinology. The local loops from the last two moments explain how skin behaves day to day. They are foundation biology, and the guide is explicit that they are no rationale for dosing anyone with a hormone. Whatever your role, a systemic pattern in the skin gets a systemic answer.
blocks.sourceNote: Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 5 clinical pearl and referral list · Safer 2011

blocks.title: A map of fourteen million cells.
blocks.narration: Fourteen million cells is the scale of the Hormone Cell Atlas, a Cambridge-led study published in Science in 2026. The team read the RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in single cells and nuclei from forty-seven human tissues, skin included. From those readings they scored each cell type for its predicted capacity to make or to receive a hormone, and they flagged unexpected sites, such as RNA for the gut hormone secretin in a type of immune cell. The Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide uses the atlas to argue that the skin, built from every major cell lineage, is plausibly one of the body's largest distributed signalling networks. The word plausibly matters. Everything in the atlas starts from RNA, and RNA tells you what a cell could make. Whether the cell actually makes and releases the hormone is the question the rest of this lesson answers.
blocks.sourceNote: Fei & Huang-Doran et al., Science 2026 · hormonecellatlas.org.uk · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 7

blocks.title: Prediction, in the authors' own words.
blocks.narration: The atlas's own portal describes its scores as 'putative and hypothesis-generating'. A few predictions were tested in cells in the paper itself; the rest are left for users to validate. Across biology, the amount of RNA for a gene is often a poor guide to how much protein a cell makes, and protein is still a step short of secretion.
blocks.sourceNote: Fei & Huang-Doran, Science 2026 · hormonecellatlas.org.uk About/FAQ, read 24 Sep 2026 · Liu 2016

stat.label: hormone and receptor genes read as RNA, cell by cell

blocks.title: Transcript, tissue or person?
blocks.narration: Findings about skin as an endocrine organ sit on different rungs of the same ladder. Before you see the answers, decide how far up each one reaches.
blocks.sourceNote: Fei 2026 · atlas portal · Ito 2005 · Phan 2021 · Horesh 2023 · Holick 1980 · Bikle 2014

blocks.title: A map to confirm, then a trial.
blocks.narration: Two habits follow from the atlas. The first concerns product claims. Topical and transdermal treatments act through receptors the skin already carries, and the skin's own enzymes change how strongly a hormone acts once it arrives, so the response in skin can differ from what the dose predicts. A receptor on a map is where an efficacy question starts, and the answer still needs a trial. The second habit concerns the physiology you think you know. The guide's testing pearl says serum vitamin D falls with sunscreen use, which the biology predicts. An independent review found that in real-life field trials, daily sunscreen did not lower blood levels, although the sunscreens tested were moderate and today's high-protection products have never been trialled. Keep recommending sun protection, and treat vitamin D as its own question.
blocks.sourceNote: Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 6–7 pearls · Neale 2019 · Fei 2026 · Bikle 2014

blocks.title: Cells that stop dividing and keep talking.
blocks.narration: Senescence begins as a safety mechanism. A cell that has taken enough damage stops dividing for good, which helps guard against cancer and is useful during wound repair. The problem is what the cell does next. It stays alive and metabolically busy and releases a mixture of inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin six and eight, enzymes that break down matrix, and growth factors. This secretory profile, the SASP, was characterised in human cells grown in the laboratory after DNA damage. In living human skin, the evidence is observational. Skin samples from older people contain more cells carrying the senescence marker p16, in both the epidermis and the dermis, and fibroblasts, keratinocytes and melanocytes can all become senescent. Researchers also caution that no single marker identifies a senescent cell with certainty, so counts depend on the marker chosen.
blocks.sourceNote: Coppé 2008 · Ressler 2006 · Ho & Dreesen 2021 · Wang & Dreesen 2018 · Haykal 2026 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 7

blocks.title: Three years of perceived age.
blocks.narration: In a Dutch cohort, people with more p16-positive cells in sun-protected arm skin had more ageing-type elastic fibres, more facial wrinkles and looked older, after allowing for their actual age. The epidermal p16-positive cells were mostly melanocytes. The study was publicly funded; one co-author worked for Unilever.
blocks.sourceNote: Waaijer 2016 (Leiden Longevity Study) · Ressler 2006

stat.label: younger-looking: fewest versus most p16-positive epidermal cells, at the same chronological age

blocks.title: Human, mouse or dish?
blocks.narration: Senescence research mixes human tissue, mice and cultured cells. For the ageing dermis the four answers point in different directions, which is why they belong in separate sentences.
blocks.sourceNote: Shuster 1975 · Varani 2006 · Fisher 2009 · Waaijer 2016 · Baker 2016 · Xu 2018 · Hickson 2019 · Chung 2019

blocks.title: The levers with trials behind them.
blocks.narration: Set the senescence story beside the interventions that have been tested in people. In Nambour, Australia, a publicly funded trial randomised 903 adults to daily or discretionary sunscreen, and over four and a half years skin ageing was about a quarter lower with daily use. Topical tretinoin has a run of randomised trials in photoaged skin that agree with one another, and the Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide rates topical retinoids first-line, grade A. Retinol has smaller trials, including one in residents in their late eighties whose fine wrinkling improved and whose biopsies showed more procollagen. Both levers protect or rebuild the dermal matrix that ultraviolet light and, it is thought, the SASP erode, and both have human outcome data. Senolytics for skin have no such data yet. Keep that order in mind when a patient asks what actually works.
blocks.sourceNote: Hughes 2013 · Sitohang 2022 · Kafi 2007 · Varani 2000 · Fisher 2002 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 5

blocks.title: 'Can a senolytic fix my skin?'
blocks.narration: Consider a fifty-eight-year-old patient, fictional and built from this lesson's evidence. She has read that senolytic supplements clear so-called zombie cells and reverse skin ageing, and she asks whether to start one she found online. She does not wear sunscreen every day. Three facts frame the conversation. Senescent cells really do accumulate in human skin, and their number tracks with wrinkles and with how old a person looks. The evidence that clearing them helps comes from mice, and the human studies so far are small pilots measuring markers in tissue. Daily sunscreen and topical retinoids, by contrast, have randomised trials with visible skin outcomes. The Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide advises keeping senolytics within clinical trials. Decide what you say first.
blocks.sourceNote: Fictional case · Waaijer 2016 · Baker 2016 · Hickson 2019 · Hughes 2013 · Sitohang 2022 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 17

units.title: Systemic hormones and the skin · three lessons

blocks.title: The face that might be a diagnosis.
blocks.narration: Most skin changes you see are ageing or lifestyle. A few are the first visible sign of endocrine disease. In three lessons you will separate them: what local and systemic hormones do to skin, what hormone therapy can and cannot do for it, and which signs belong with an endocrinologist.
blocks.sourceNote: Hormones and Peptides for Skin · Module 02

blocks.title: The skin regenerates its own cortisol.
blocks.narration: Picture the skin as a small endocrine organ with its own stress axis. Skin cells make CRH and ACTH, the same signals that drive the adrenal glands, and they carry the receptors to respond to them. They also carry an enzyme called eleven beta HSD one, which turns inactive cortisone back into active cortisol inside the cell. In human skin samples that enzyme works harder with age and in sun-exposed skin, and it sets local cortisol independently of the level in the blood. Cortisol slows collagen production in dermal fibroblasts, and mice bred without the enzyme kept their dermal thickness as they aged. Hold all of this in the mechanism register. It comes from biopsies, cultured cells and mice, and it says nothing yet about how a patient's face will age.
blocks.sourceNote: Slominski & Wortsman 2000 · Tiganescu 2011, 2013 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 8

blocks.title: 11β-HSD1: four separate answers.
blocks.narration: Local cortisol regeneration is a real and interesting mechanism. Each register below answers a different question, and blending them produces the line you will hear online: that blocking cortisol in the skin reverses ageing.
blocks.sourceNote: Tiganescu 2011, 2013 · Ajjan 2022 · ClinicalTrials.gov and Drugs@FDA, checked 24 Sep 2026

blocks.title: Which features point to Cushing's?
blocks.narration: Cushing's syndrome shares most of its features with ordinary weight gain, poor sleep and stress. The Endocrine Society's diagnostic guideline separates the few that discriminate from the many that are common. Before you see its verdicts, sort these eight.
blocks.sourceNote: Endocrine Society guideline, Nieman 2008, Table 1 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 8

blocks.title: Rare, and usually from a prescription.
blocks.narration: Endogenous Cushing's syndrome is uncommon: European population studies put it at two to three new cases per million people a year. The commonest cause of Cushing's syndrome is iatrogenic, from glucocorticoids given as medicine. The Endocrine Society therefore asks for a drug history first, covering tablets, inhalers, injections and creams, including skin-bleaching products, and recommends testing when features are multiple and progressive.
blocks.sourceNote: Endocrine Society guideline, Nieman 2008 — introduction and recommendations 3.1–3.3

stat.label: new cases of endogenous Cushing's syndrome per million people per year (European population studies)

blocks.title: Reassure the many, refer the few.
blocks.narration: Here is how that plays out when a patient asks about cortisol face. Begin with a drug history, because the commonest cause of cortisol excess is a glucocorticoid someone is already using. The guideline names the easy ones to miss, such as skin-bleaching creams, herbal tonics, and joint or nerve injections. Then look for the four features that shift the odds, meaning easy bruising, a plethoric face, weakness in the hips and shoulders, and wide reddish-purple striae. Without them, the Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide reads most puffiness as sleep, alcohol, salt and fluid, and the Endocrine Society advises against testing everyone. With them, and especially when they are progressing, the patient needs formal testing and an endocrinologist. A cortisol supplement or a mail-order saliva panel answers the wrong question.
blocks.sourceNote: Endocrine Society guideline 2008, recommendations 3.1–3.5 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 8 clinical pearl

blocks.title: Estrogen and the dermis.
blocks.narration: Estrogen is the hormone the guide says dominates the visible ageing of women's skin, so start with what it does in the dermis. Skin carries estrogen receptors in sun-protected and sun-damaged sites alike. In a vehicle-controlled study, two weeks of topical estradiol raised collagen production in the hip skin of postmenopausal women; in photoaged forearm and facial skin, the same treatment made no measurable difference. Small biopsy studies from the nineteen eighties and nineties found that skin collagen and thickness fall after menopause, and that the fall follows years since the last period more closely than birthdays. Keep two questions apart as you go. One is what estrogen does in the dermis. The other is whether giving it changes how a face ages, and those answers come from different trials.
blocks.sourceNote: Rittié 2008 · Thornton 2013 · Brincat 1985 · Affinito 1999 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 9

blocks.title: One to two per cent a year.
blocks.narration: In small biopsy studies of postmenopausal women, skin collagen content and skin thickness fell by about 1–2% a year, in step with bone mass, and followed years since menopause more than age. Reviews, and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide, quote a steeper early loss of up to 30% in the first five years. That figure traces to the same small studies, and a check of their abstracts in September 2026 did not find it stated.
blocks.sourceNote: Brincat 1985, 1987 · Affinito 1999 · Thornton 2013

stat.label: fall in skin collagen content and thickness per year after menopause (small biopsy studies)

blocks.title: Biopsy gains, mirror results.
blocks.narration: Hormone therapy has two kinds of trial behind it. Small trials measure the dermis; larger trials measure the face. They point in different directions, so read them separately. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide grades the skin benefit B; the North American Menopause Society rates the same evidence 'limited or inconsistent'. This course grades the structural gains C and teaches the negative wrinkle trials alongside them.
blocks.sourceNote: Maheux 1994 · Sauerbronn 2000 · Phillips 2008 · Owen 2016 · Pivazyan 2023 · Creidi 1994 · Ashcroft 1999 · NAMS 2022

blocks.title: Symptoms and bone. Skin is a bystander.
blocks.narration: Where does that leave hormone therapy for skin? In the United States, as of February 2026, the approved uses of menopausal hormone therapy are hot flashes, vaginal and vulvar symptoms, and for some products the prevention of bone loss. In late 2025 the FDA asked manufacturers to remove heart, breast cancer and dementia statements from the boxed warning, and it approved the first revised labels in February 2026. Skin still appears nowhere among the uses. The menopause society's 2022 position statement finds the balance favourable for symptoms and bone when therapy starts before sixty or within ten years of menopause, and it finds too little evidence for compounded bioidentical hormones. Low-dose vaginal estrogen for genitourinary symptoms is the one use aimed at the tissue itself. For the face, daily sunscreen and a prescription retinoid carry better evidence than any hormone. Treat symptoms on their merits, and count any skin change as a bonus.
blocks.sourceNote: FDA, 10 Nov 2025 and 12 Feb 2026 · 21 CFR 310.530 · NAMS 2022, 2020 · Manson 2013 · Hughes 2013 · Renova label

blocks.title: Some syndromes show on the skin first.
blocks.narration: Some endocrine syndromes are written on the skin years before the glands give them away. In multiple endocrine neoplasia type one, most patients in one careful series had several facial angiofibromas, the same lesions seen in tuberous sclerosis, along with collagenomas on the trunk. In Carney complex, usually caused by inactivating variants in the PRKAR1A gene, freckle-like lentigines cluster on the lips, eyelids and the corners of the eyes, alongside blue naevi and small skin myxomas. The same patients can develop myxomas in the heart and cortisol-secreting adrenal disease. In MEN two A, an itchy, rippled, darkened patch between the shoulder blades, called cutaneous lichen amyloidosis, can appear long before medullary thyroid cancer. Each of these is a referral finding, and none of them is yours to diagnose alone.
blocks.sourceNote: Darling 1997 · Kirschner 2000 · Correa 2015 · Stanescu 2024 · Lause 2017 · the guide's inherited-syndromes chapter

blocks.title: Eighty-eight per cent.
blocks.narration: In a consecutive series of 32 people with MEN1 examined at the US National Institutes of Health, 88% had multiple facial angiofibromas and 72% had collagenomas. The angiofibromas were clinically and histologically identical to those of tuberous sclerosis. The authors concluded that angiofibromas in someone without tuberous sclerosis call for biochemical testing for MEN1.
blocks.sourceNote: Darling et al., Arch Dermatol 1997

stat.label: of 32 people with MEN1 had multiple facial angiofibromas

blocks.title: The everyday endocrine signs.
blocks.narration: Most of the endocrine skin signs you will actually meet come from common conditions. New, generalised darkening, most obvious in skin creases such as the palms, in scars, on the gums and on sun-exposed skin, can be the sign of primary adrenal insufficiency. In a patient who is also unwell, the Endocrine Society recommends testing, and a suspected adrenal crisis is treated before the results come back, because delay raises the risk of death. Hirsutism that arrives quickly, keeps progressing, or comes with a deeper voice or clitoromegaly makes an androgen-secreting tumour more likely, and more than half of those tumours are malignant. Velvety dark plaques in the neck folds track insulin resistance. Firm plaques on the shins point to Graves' disease, and cold, dry, coarse skin suggests an underactive thyroid. The skin shows you which door to knock on.
blocks.sourceNote: Endocrine Society guidelines: Bornstein 2016, Martin 2018 · Lause 2017 · the guide's ch. 5 referral list

blocks.title: Where does this skin finding go?
blocks.narration: Seven presentations from an aesthetic list, and three routes. Your job is to route the finding, not to make the diagnosis. The verdict and the source behind each appear as you answer.
blocks.sourceNote: Endocrine Society guidelines 2008, 2016, 2018 · Darling 1997 · Stanescu 2024 · the guide's ch. 5 referral list and algorithms

blocks.title: Freckles before the wedding.
blocks.narration: Consider a fictional patient, built from this lesson's evidence. She is twenty-nine and wants the freckles on her lips and at the corners of her eyes lasered before her wedding. While you examine her you notice a soft, skin-coloured bump on one eyelid. She mentions that her father had a heart tumour removed in his thirties. Pigmented spots at the corners of the eyes are seen in Carney complex and Peutz–Jeghers syndrome, and small skin myxomas favour the eyelids and ears. In Carney complex, tumours of the heart cause more than half of the deaths, which is why screening matters once the diagnosis is suspected. The laser itself may be harmless. The question is what the skin is telling you. Choose your first move.
blocks.sourceNote: Correa 2015 · Kirschner 2000 · the guide's inherited-syndromes chapter

units.title: Fat, incretins and the ageing face · three lessons

blocks.title: The face changes when the fat does.
blocks.narration: Facial shape depends on fat as much as on collagen. In three lessons you will separate what is known about the skin's own fat, sugar damage to the dermis, weight-loss drugs and the gut from what is still mechanism, marketing or an open question.
blocks.sourceNote: Hormones and Peptides for Skin · Module 03

blocks.title: The skin keeps its own fat.
blocks.narration: Most people picture skin fat as one layer under the dermis. There is a second, thinner layer inside the reticular dermis itself, called dermal white adipose tissue. In mice, this layer expands rapidly after a Staphylococcus aureus infection, and its new fat cells release cathelicidin, an antimicrobial peptide. Older mice lose much of that capacity, through TGF-beta signalling. Human skin arranges this fat differently, in small cones around hair follicles, and human acne lesions contain preadipocytes around the follicle that make cathelicidin. What the layer contributes to human skin ageing has not yet been measured. So hold two things apart when you hear about skin fat. The defence story is strong in mice and emerging in people. The ageing story in people is still a proposal.
blocks.sourceNote: Zhang 2015, 2019 · Chen 2019 · Kruglikov & Scherer 2016 · O'Neill 2022 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 11

blocks.title: Fat that holds the face up.
blocks.narration: Cadaver dissection shows that the face's subcutaneous fat sits in separate compartments, and facial ageing is partly how each compartment changes. Weight shows the same thing from the outside. In a study of 186 pairs of identical twins, the twin with the higher body-mass index looked older before about age 40 and younger after it.
blocks.sourceNote: Rohrich & Pessa 2007 · Guyuron 2009

stat.label: pairs of identical twins compared for facial ageing

blocks.title: Sugar that sticks to collagen.
blocks.narration: Glycation is chemistry before it is biology. Reducing sugars attach to the amino groups of proteins, rearrange into more stable products, and end as advanced glycation end products, known as AGEs. Dermal collagen lasts for years, so it collects AGEs, and they form cross-links that make the matrix stiffer. AGEs also bind a receptor called RAGE, which in laboratory studies switches on inflammatory signalling and enzymes that break down matrix. Keep the registers apart here. The chemistry, and the build-up of AGEs in human skin, are well documented. The idea that AGEs cause the wrinkles and laxity you see in clinic rests on laboratory and animal work plus human associations. The Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide rates the structural and inflammatory effects grade B. This course grades the causal link D, and the next moment shows why.
blocks.sourceNote: Gkogkolou & Böhm 2012 · Dyer 1993 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 13

blocks.title: Fifteen years on the same collagen.
blocks.narration: Human skin collagen turns over slowly; tissue analysis puts its half-life at about 15 years. In skin biopsies, glycoxidation products in collagen rose about five-fold between ages 20 and 85, and were up to twice as high in type 1 diabetes. Skin autofluorescence, a non-invasive reading, correlates moderately with those biopsy measures and was validated in non-pigmented skin.
blocks.sourceNote: Verzijl 2000 · Dyer 1993 · Meerwaldt 2004

stat.label: estimated half-life of human skin collagen

blocks.title: Two gut hormones, re-engineered.
blocks.narration: After a meal, the gut releases two hormones called incretins, GLP-1 and GIP. Both amplify insulin release when glucose is high, and GLP-1 also slows the stomach and reduces appetite. Native GLP-1 lasts only minutes in the blood before an enzyme breaks it down, so the drug molecules are engineered to last far longer. Semaglutide activates the GLP-1 receptor. Tirzepatide activates both the GIP and the GLP-1 receptors. Those are the mechanisms. The regulatory facts sit in a separate register. In the United States, as of September 2026, both molecules are FDA-approved drugs, sold under one brand name for type 2 diabetes and another for chronic weight management, with further indications for the heart, the liver and sleep apnoea. The face appears nowhere on those labels, and that is where this lesson begins.
blocks.sourceNote: Drucker 2018 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 12 · Peptide Pocket Guide · US labels

blocks.title: Approved for what, exactly?
blocks.narration: The facial changes in this lesson happen to people taking approved drugs for approved reasons. Know the indications, and their dates, before you discuss the side effects. Status below is for the US, from FDA records checked in September 2026; UK and EU status is being mapped for this course.
blocks.sourceNote: US labels via DailyMed (2026) · Drugs@FDA · FDA, current 1 Sep 2026 · Ashraf 2024

blocks.title: Large trials, measured on the scale.
blocks.narration: In STEP-1, 1,961 adults without diabetes lost a mean 14.9% of body weight on semaglutide over 68 weeks, against 2.4% on placebo. In SURMOUNT-1, 2,539 adults lost 15.0% to 20.9% on tirzepatide over 72 weeks, depending on dose, against 3.1% on placebo. Both Hormonaly guides grade weight management A. Across 35 randomized trials of incretin drugs, a median of about 28% of the weight lost was muscle-related tissue.
blocks.sourceNote: Wilding 2021 · Jastreboff 2022 · Batsis 2026

blocks.title: 'Ozempic face', answer by answer.
blocks.narration: The phrase bundles four kinds of statement. Kept apart, they tell a patient far more than the headline does.
blocks.sourceNote: Sharma 2025 · Rao 2026 · Daneshgaran 2025 · US labels 2026 · Paschou 2025

blocks.title: Counsel before, record during, refer when asked.
blocks.narration: Three moments matter in practice. Before treatment starts, raise facial volume change and hair shedding as possibilities, especially with older patients, as the Hormonaly guide advises, and record that you did. During treatment, photograph the face with consent so that change is measured rather than remembered, and support the protein intake and resistance training the guide recommends to protect lean mass. When a patient asks for help with the face, refer to a qualified aesthetic or dermatology colleague. The published advice on restoring volume after drug-driven weight loss is expert opinion, the main consensus statement was developed with industry involvement, and randomized trials of fillers and devices in these patients are registered with no results yet. Whatever your role, decisions about the medicine itself stay with the prescriber and the patient.
blocks.sourceNote: Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 12, 14 · Nikolis 2025 · ClinicalTrials.gov, checked 24 Sep 2026

blocks.title: Ten months in, and unhappy with the mirror.
blocks.narration: Picture a fifty-eight-year-old patient, fictional and built from this lesson's evidence. She has taken semaglutide for obesity for ten months, prescribed by her physician, and has lost eighteen percent of her body weight. Her blood pressure and glucose have improved. She is distressed by hollow cheeks and new looseness along the jaw, and she is finding more hair in her brush. She asks whether she should stop the injections. Consider what the evidence says. In the studies so far, facial volume loss tracks the amount of weight lost. Hair loss is a labelled side effect, reported more often in women and linked to weight reduction. The drug was prescribed for a medical reason, and that reason is going well. Decide how you would answer her.
blocks.sourceNote: Sharma 2025 · Rao 2026 · Wegovy label 2026 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 12

blocks.title: Inflammation that comes with age.
blocks.narration: Ageing brings a slow rise in background inflammation, called inflammaging. It is low-grade and sterile, and in older adults higher IL-6 and C-reactive protein predict frailty, disability and death. One proposed source is the gut. In mice, a high-fat diet raises bacterial lipopolysaccharide in the blood, and infusing that endotoxin reproduces weight gain and insulin resistance. In twelve healthy men, a single high-fat meal raised plasma endotoxin within four hours. That is the mechanism usually called metabolic endotoxaemia, or leaky gut. The human evidence stops short of the skin. Measuring gut permeability is difficult, and a leading review concludes that it is still unproven whether restoring the barrier improves disease outside the gut. Hold that line as you look at what patients are sold.
blocks.sourceNote: Franceschi 2000 · Ferrucci & Fabbri 2018 · Cani 2007 · Erridge 2007 · Camilleri 2019

blocks.title: Thirty-nine trials of probiotics for eczema.
blocks.narration: An independent Cochrane review pooled 39 randomized trials, with 2,599 participants, of oral probiotics for eczema. Probiotics probably make little or no difference to patient-rated symptoms, and investigator-rated severity fell by less than the minimum clinically important difference. A 2024 European task-force meta-analysis in children without food allergy reported a significant fall in severity scores.
blocks.sourceNote: Makrgeorgou 2018 (Cochrane) · Vassilopoulou 2024 · Suez 2019

stat.label: in the Cochrane review of oral probiotics for treating eczema

blocks.title: What has been tested on skin?
blocks.narration: Six things patients bring you under the heading 'gut health for skin'. One at a time, decide what stands behind each.

blocks.title: Diet first, a bottle last.
blocks.narration: Patients often link their skin to their gut. Start where the evidence is. Diet quality, treatment of metabolic disease and the established treatment for the skin condition itself all come first. Be careful with tests. A widely used commercial zonulin assay was shown to detect proteins other than zonulin, so a result cannot tell you whether a gut is leaky. Be careful with products too. Probiotics are strain-specific, and their effects on eczema are small at best. The Hormonaly guide gives the popular gut-repair stack of glutamine, zinc carnosine and BPC-157 a grade of D. As of September 2026, in the United States, BPC-157 remains off the 503A bulks list after the July advisory-committee review. Investigational peptides come last, if at all. Whatever your role, name the evidence type before you name the product.
blocks.sourceNote: Scheffler 2018 · Camilleri 2019 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 16 · FDA PCAC, July 2026

options.text: Semaglutide ages the face by acting on facial fat, so the label should carry a facial warning.

Facial volume loss on incretins: fat loss deflates facial compartments (mechanism); small observational studies tie it to the amount of weight lost (human evidence); US labels list hair loss but not facial change (regulatory status); whether the drugs act directly on facial fat is untested (open question).

units.title: Matrix peptides and wound healing · three lessons

blocks.title: The peptide your patient already bought.
blocks.narration: Most skin peptides reach your clinic before any evidence does. In three lessons you will sort them by what the human trials actually show, who paid for those trials, and where each one stands with the regulator.
blocks.sourceNote: Hormones and Peptides for Skin · Module 04

blocks.title: How will you use this module?
blocks.narration: The evidence, grades and regulatory status are the same for everyone. What changes is the 'what you do next' at the end of each lesson, so it fits what your licence lets you do.
blocks.sourceNote: Audience decision, Omar Saleem 2026-09-22

blocks.title: A plasma tripeptide with a copper habit.
blocks.narration: Start with the molecule. GHK is a three-amino-acid peptide that circulates in human plasma; it was first described in 1973. It binds copper readily, and the copper complex, GHK-Cu, is what skin-care labels mean when they say copper peptide. The proposed mechanism is that GHK-Cu delivers copper to enzymes that build and protect the dermal matrix, such as lysyl oxidase and superoxide dismutase, and shifts gene expression toward wound healing. Two things to hold on to. First, this is a mechanism, which explains why the peptide might work and leaves open whether it does. Second, most of this literature was written by the group that discovered the peptide. Keep both in mind when you reach the trials.
blocks.sourceNote: Pickart & Thaler 1973 · Pickart 2008, 2015, 2018 · Peptide Pocket Guide

blocks.title: One indexed randomized trial.
blocks.narration: A search of PubMed in September 2026 found one randomized controlled trial of topical GHK-Cu in human skin: 2006, healing after CO₂ laser resurfacing. The cosmetic trials cited for anti-ageing claims are manufacturer-sponsored and not indexed. Both Hormonaly guides grade topical use C.
blocks.sourceNote: Miller 2006 · Peptide Pocket Guide · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology

stat.label: indexed randomized trial of topical GHK-Cu in human skin

blocks.title: Keep the four answers apart.
blocks.narration: Every peptide question has four separate answers. For GHK-Cu they point in different directions, which is exactly why they must not be blended into one sentence.
blocks.sourceNote: Registry m04 · FDA 503A category list, updated 14 May 2026

blocks.title: Serum yes, syringe no.
blocks.narration: Here is what that means in the room. Topical GHK-Cu is a reasonable cosmetic conversation, as long as you describe the evidence honestly: small trials, modest effects, grade C. Injected GHK-Cu is not the same product in a stronger form. There are no randomized trials of injection, injection-site pain and rash are common because copper irritates tissue, and in the United States the injectable route sits outside the Category 1 listing that covers non-injectable use. Whatever your role, name the route every time you talk about this peptide.
blocks.sourceNote: Peptide Pocket Guide · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 15 · FDA 503A categories

blocks.title: Three families, one question: who ran the trial?
blocks.narration: Lesson two covers three families that fill the cosmetic and supplement shelves. Signal peptides, like palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, sold as Matrixyl, are fragments of matrix proteins meant to tell fibroblasts to make more collagen. SNAP-25 mimics, Argireline and its longer cousin SNAP-8, copy part of a nerve-terminal protein that botulinum toxin targets; the idea is a gentle, topical version of that effect. And oral collagen peptides are swallowed, not applied. Every one of these has trials behind it. As you go through them, keep asking one question before any other: who ran the trial, and who paid for it.
blocks.sourceNote: Lupo & Cole 2007 · Lintner & Peschard 2000 · Blanes-Mira 2002 · Errante 2020

blocks.title: A trial, or a brochure?
blocks.narration: Five products from two families, and what each promises on the label. Before you see a grade, decide what actually stands behind each one.
blocks.sourceNote: Robinson 2005 · Wang 2013 · Aruan 2023 · Errante 2020 · Pocket Guide

blocks.title: Twenty-three trials, split by who paid.
blocks.narration: Pooled, oral collagen trials show better hydration, elasticity and wrinkle scores, and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide grades them C. A 2025 meta-analysis split the same kind of trials by funding and by quality. The benefit appeared only in pharmaceutical-funded and low-quality trials. Unfunded and high-quality trials showed no effect.
blocks.sourceNote: Myung & Park, Am J Med 2025 · Pu 2023 · de Miranda 2021 · Kim 2018

stat.label: in the 2025 meta-analysis that split oral-collagen trials by funding and quality

blocks.title: Cosmetic, supplement, drug: three rulebooks.
blocks.narration: Now the regulatory register, stated for the United States. Cosmetic peptides are cosmetic ingredients, not drugs; their safety is assessed under a cosmetics framework, and nobody has to prove they work before they are sold. Oral collagen is sold as a dietary supplement, so it cannot claim to treat a disease, and what is in the tub varies from brand to brand. That is the whole reason the funding question matters here. When no regulator asks for efficacy, the only efficacy data are the trials someone chose to pay for. UK and EU rules are being mapped for this course and will be added.
blocks.sourceNote: Bjerke 2026 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology · Pocket Guide

blocks.title: Rodents, a fragment, and a tripeptide.
blocks.narration: Lesson three moves from the cosmetic shelf to the peptides patients buy online and inject. BPC-157 is a fifteen-residue peptide first described in 1993. Its evidence is a large rodent literature, most of it from one research group, and uncontrolled human case series. TB-500 is sold as thymosin, but when anti-doping chemists analysed the product they found a seven-residue fragment, residues seventeen to twenty-three of thymosin beta-four. That fragment has never been tested in a trial. KPV is the last three amino acids of alpha-MSH; it calms inflammation in mouse colitis models, and there is no randomized human trial of it for anything. All three have plausible mechanisms, and none has a controlled human trial.
blocks.sourceNote: Sikiric 2018 · Seiwerth 2021 · Lee 2021 · Esposito 2012 · Dalmasso 2008

blocks.title: One abstract, no published trial.
blocks.narration: As of September 2026 no randomized efficacy trial of BPC-157 in people has been published in full. FDA's July 2026 briefing found one randomized, placebo-controlled trial reported only as a 2005 meeting abstract: 53 people with ulcerative colitis, two weeks of treatment, and no significant difference from placebo. ClinicalTrials.gov adds a 2015 phase 1 safety study that never posted results, a completed 2025 single-arm product study with no results posted, and a randomized phase 1 trial after rotator-cuff surgery due to start in 2027.
blocks.sourceNote: ClinicalTrials.gov, checked 24 Sep 2026 · McGuire 2025 · Mayfield 2026

blocks.title: Two trials, one peptide: LL-37.
blocks.narration: LL-37, the skin's own cathelicidin, is the one repair peptide with two randomized trials in hard-to-heal venous leg ulcers. Read them in order.
blocks.sourceNote: Grönberg 2014 · Mahlapuu 2021 · Schauber & Gallo 2008

blocks.title: Where does it stand in the US?
blocks.narration: Three US categories, dated to the FDA's category list of 14 May 2026 and the advisory-committee meeting of 23–24 July 2026. The committee's votes are advice; FDA must still act through rulemaking before anything joins the bulks list. FDA has sent warning letters naming GHK-Cu and BPC-157 on exactly this basis.

blocks.title: New dark patches, three months into 'GLOW'.
blocks.narration: A fictional case, built from this lesson's evidence. A forty-six-year-old patient has been injecting a research-use-only blend sold as GLOW for three months: GHK-Cu, BPC-157 and TB-500 in one vial. She likes her skin and asks about carrying on. You notice new, patchy darkening on her face and forearms. The blend has no controlled human trials, it is made outside good manufacturing practice, and the Hormonaly guide treats new pigmentation on these products as a red flag. Impurity and mislabelling are documented for similar online products; the Hormonaly guide states that heavy-metal contamination is documented in these products, but the published analysis behind that statement could not be found. Decide what you do first.

modules.objective: By the end, you can appraise the neuroendocrinology of the hair follicle and melanocortin receptor system, contrasting FDA-approved therapeutics with the clinical and oncologic hazards of unregulated peptides.

units.title: Follicle, pigment and melanocortins · three lessons

blocks.title: A spray for the scalp, a tan in a vial.
blocks.narration: Two requests reach aesthetic clinics well ahead of their evidence: a peptide to regrow hair and an injection to tan. In three lessons you will see how the follicle and the pigment system run on the skin's own hormones, why one melanocortin drug is approved while its gray-market cousin is approved nowhere, and how to grade the hair peptides patients bring to you.
blocks.sourceNote: Hormones and Peptides for Skin · Module 05

blocks.title: A follicle that runs its own hormones.
blocks.narration: Each hair follicle behaves like a small gland. When researchers keep human scalp follicles alive in culture, the follicles answer corticotropin-releasing hormone the way the pituitary and adrenal glands do. They make ACTH and alpha-MSH, they secrete cortisol, and cortisol-like signals feed back to switch the stimulus down. The same follicles run a growth hormone and IGF-1 loop of their own. On the scalp, an enzyme called five-alpha-reductase turns testosterone into dihydrotestosterone, and in genetically susceptible follicles that hormone drives the gradual shrinking behind pattern hair loss. Growing follicles also hide from the immune system. When that protection collapses, immune cells attack the hair bulb, and the result is alopecia areata. Most of this biology comes from tissue kept alive outside the body, so hold it as mechanism, a reason something might matter in patients.
blocks.sourceNote: Ito 2005 · Horesh 2023 · Bertolini 2020 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 6

blocks.title: Two trials, 1,200 adults, one approval.
blocks.narration: When immune privilege fails, the attack depends on cytokine signals that JAK inhibitors interrupt. Two randomized phase 3 trials tested oral baricitinib in 1,200 adults with severe alopecia areata. In the US, FDA approved baricitinib for adults with severe alopecia areata on 13 June 2022. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide grades it A.
blocks.sourceNote: King 2022 (BRAVE-AA1 and -AA2) · FDA approval letter, 13 Jun 2022

stat.label: adults with severe alopecia areata in the two phase 3 trials of baricitinib (2022)

blocks.title: Four questions before any product.
blocks.narration: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide's first-pass hair-loss workup asks four questions in order. Each yes points to a different condition and a different next step.
blocks.sourceNote: Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology · hair-loss workup algorithm and ch. 5 referral list

blocks.title: Work up the hair loss before anyone mentions a peptide.
blocks.narration: Most requests for a hair peptide skip the diagnosis. Start with the pattern, ask about a trigger, look for patches and nail pitting, and look for signs of androgen excess. Check ferritin and thyroid function every time, and send a scarring pattern for biopsy. The approved options already carry strong evidence. Pooled randomized trials support topical minoxidil in men and women and finasteride in men. In the United States minoxidil is sold over the counter, while finasteride for hair loss needs a prescription. Severe or fast-spreading alopecia areata belongs with a dermatologist, where a JAK inhibitor is an approved option for adults. Whatever your role, the workup comes before the product.
blocks.sourceNote: Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology · Adil 2017 · Drugs@FDA (checked 24 Sep 2026) · FDA approval letter 2022

blocks.title: Shedding after the baby.
blocks.narration: One question to close lesson 5.1.
blocks.sourceNote: Lesson 5.1

quiz.prompt: A 32-year-old woman asks for a compounded peptide scalp spray. Diffuse shedding began three months after she gave birth; there are no patches and no signs of androgen excess. What comes first?

blocks.title: Five receptors, one family of hormones.
blocks.narration: Pigment starts with hormones the skin makes for itself. Skin cells produce a precursor called POMC and cut it into ACTH, alpha-MSH and beta-endorphin, and the same cells carry the receptors that answer them. There are five melanocortin receptors. MC1R sets the pigment of skin and hair. MC2R is the adrenal receptor for ACTH. MC3R and MC4R work in the brain on appetite, and central receptors also drive sexual responses. MC5R governs sebum. Researchers caution that the real map is messier, with receptors turning up in more tissues than the textbook suggests. For this lesson one idea matters most. A drug that stays on MC1R mostly changes pigment, and a drug that reaches the brain's receptors brings other effects with it.
blocks.sourceNote: Slominski & Wortsman 2000 · Laiho & Murray 2022 · Böhm 2025

blocks.title: One receptor family, two very different molecules.
blocks.narration: Afamelanotide and Melanotan II are both synthetic relatives of α-MSH. Compare them register by register and the resemblance ends at the receptor.
blocks.sourceNote: Langendonk 2015 · EMA Scenesse EPAR · FDA Scenesse label (Aug 2024) · Dorr 1996 · Wessells 1998 · Böhm 2025

blocks.title: Sixty-nine hours against forty-one.
blocks.narration: Erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP) is a rare disorder in which sunlight causes acute, severe pain. In the US phase 3 trial, adults on afamelanotide spent a median 69.4 hours in direct sunlight without pain over six months, against 40.8 hours on placebo. The European trial also showed more pain-free time and fewer phototoxic reactions. Both trials were funded by the manufacturer.
blocks.sourceNote: Langendonk 2015 (NEJM) · FDA Scenesse label, Aug 2024 · EMA EPAR

stat.label: median pain-free hours in direct sunlight over six months, afamelanotide vs placebo (US phase 3 trial, 94 adults with EPP)

blocks.title: What the case reports show.
blocks.narration: Now the harms, and the kind of evidence behind them. Everything here comes from case reports and reviews, which tell you what can happen and leave open how often it does. In the skin, existing moles darken and grow, new moles erupt in crops, some of them atypical under the microscope, and dark bands can appear in the nails. At least five melanomas have been reported during or after Melanotan use. Each patient had other risk factors, such as fair skin, sunbed use or a family history, so causation is unproven, and the concern rests on a drug that pushes melanocytes to multiply. Beyond the skin, reports describe priapism that needed surgery, a stimulant-like toxic reaction with muscle breakdown and kidney injury, and a brain swelling syndrome that FDA lists among the published serious events.
blocks.sourceNote: Habbema 2017 · Cardones 2009 · Paurobally 2013 · Hjuler 2014 · Mallory 2021 · Nelson 2012 · FDA compounding safety page

blocks.title: New moles after a summer of tanning shots.
blocks.narration: Her booking says skin quality. This patient is fictional, built from the lesson's evidence. She is twenty-seven, and she mentions that she has been injecting a tanning peptide bought online for three months. She has noticed darker moles, several new small ones, and a dark stripe along one fingernail. Her mother had melanoma. The product is almost certainly Melanotan II, approved nowhere and of unknown strength and purity. New and changing moles and nail pigmentation are exactly the harms described in the reports, and in one patient followed with dermoscopy the changes made moles hard to tell from melanoma. The endocrinology guide treats a family history of melanoma as an absolute contraindication. Pick the move that comes first.
blocks.sourceNote: Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 15 · Cardones 2009 · Mang 2012 · Böhm 2025 · FDA Scenesse label

blocks.title: Three regulators, one answer.
blocks.narration: Each statement below is dated, because regulatory status changes. None of the three regulators has approved Melanotan II, and each has put its concerns on the record. UK and EU mapping for the rest of this course is still in progress.
blocks.sourceNote: FDA compounding safety page (22 Apr 2026) · MHRA FOI 24/274 (17 Apr 2024) · TGA safety advisory (17 Aug 2026)

blocks.narration: One question to close lesson 5.2.

quiz.prompt: A patient says, 'Afamelanotide is approved, so Melanotan II is basically the same drug.' What is the accurate reply?

blocks.title: A Wnt switch and a zinc question.
blocks.narration: Two peptides are sold for hair, and both arrive with better stories than data. PTD-DBM joins a cell-penetrating fragment borrowed from an HIV protein to a short decoy sequence. Inside follicle cells, the decoy keeps a protein called CXXC5 from binding its partner, Dishevelled, and that releases a brake on Wnt signalling, a pathway involved in hair regrowth. In mice, hair regrew faster and follicles formed in healed wounds. The work came from the developer's own group. Zinc thymulin is a thymic hormone that becomes active only when zinc binds to it. How it might help hair has never been defined, and nobody has shown whether any effect would come from the peptide or from the zinc. Hold both as mechanism, and look for the human trial.
blocks.sourceNote: Lee 2017 (J Invest Dermatol) · Dardenne 1982 · Peptide Pocket Guide

blocks.title: Zero trials in people.
blocks.narration: As of September 2026, PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov list no human trial of PTD-DBM, published or registered. Its evidence is one 2017 study in mice and human scalp tissue from the developer's group, whose senior author is affiliated with a biotech company. A 2025 review's summary speaks of 'clinical efficacy', yet the review's own text describes PTD-DBM results in mouse models only.
blocks.sourceNote: PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov, searched 24 Sep 2026 · Lee 2017 · Mehta 2025

stat.label: human trials of PTD-DBM, published or registered (September 2026)

blocks.title: Approved, or unproven?
blocks.narration: Five things patients use or ask about for hair, with what each is claimed to do. Decide what stands behind each one before you see a grade.
blocks.sourceNote: Adil 2017 · King 2022 · Drugs@FDA · Lee 2017 · FDA 503A categories (14 May 2026) · Pocket Guide

blocks.title: When the request is a compounded hair spray.
blocks.narration: Stated for the United States, the regulatory picture is short. On FDA's category lists of the fourteenth of May, twenty twenty-six, thymulin acetate sits in Category 3, meaning it was nominated without enough information for FDA to evaluate, and it falls outside the enforcement discretion that Category 1 substances receive. PTD-DBM appears on none of the three lists. Neither substance is on the 503A bulks list itself. The evidence grade for both is D. So when a patient asks for a compounded hair spray, give the grade plainly, go back to the diagnosis, and describe the approved options and what they can offer. units.title: The growth-hormone axis and the skin · three lessons

blocks.title: Real endocrinology, borrowed for marketing.
blocks.narration: Growth hormone and IGF-1 genuinely shape skin, and one peptide on this axis has approval-grade trials. Most of what patients are offered has much less behind it. In three lessons you will separate the physiology from the promise, the approved from the anecdotal, and the side-effects you can see from the risks nobody has measured.
blocks.sourceNote: Hormones and Peptides for Skin · Module 06

blocks.title: Two hormones, two layers of skin.
blocks.narration: Two layers of skin listen to two different parts of the same axis. Growth hormone speaks mainly to the dermis. Its receptor is expressed more on fibroblasts than on keratinocytes, and in culture growth hormone increases fibroblast numbers and supports collagen synthesis, sometimes directly and sometimes through IGF-1. The epidermis listens to IGF-1. Keratinocytes carry the IGF-1 receptor, their neighbours in the dermis supply the hormone, and in culture IGF-1 makes keratinocytes divide where growth hormone on its own does nothing. Human hair follicles even keep a small growth-hormone loop running when they are cultured outside the body. With age, growth-hormone pulses and IGF-1 fall steadily, a change called the somatopause. Hold all of this as mechanism. It explains why the axis could matter for skin. Whether changing it helps a patient is a separate question, and the trials answer it.
blocks.sourceNote: Tavakkol 1992 · Edmondson 2003 · Horesh 2023 · Veldhuis 2008 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 2 and 6

blocks.title: A much-cited skin result, read again.
blocks.narration: In 1990 a much-cited New England Journal of Medicine study gave growth hormone for six months to 12 healthy men over 60, with nine untreated men for comparison and no placebo. Lean mass rose and fat fell. Skin thickness rose 7.1%, with P = 0.07, short of statistical significance. A small 1996 randomized trial in 28 older men found 15% more collagen laid down in implanted wound tubes on GH, a laboratory surrogate for repair.
blocks.sourceNote: Rudman 1990 · Papadakis 1996

stat.label: rise in skin thickness in 12 older men given growth hormone for six months (1990)

blocks.title: Deficiency is a diagnosis. Decline is ageing.
blocks.narration: Here the physiology meets the waiting room. A patient in their fifties has read that growth hormone falls with age and asks whether topping it up would help their skin. The trials in healthy older adults answer that. Pooled, they show about two kilograms less fat and two kilograms more lean mass, with more swelling, joint pain, carpal tunnel symptoms and a drift towards diabetes, while strength and stamina change little. Graded on those trials the evidence is B, consistent and independent though small, and the Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide gives its advice against treatment an A. Both land in the same place. Growth hormone treats a diagnosed deficiency and a short list of approved conditions. In the United States, distributing it for anti-ageing is a federal offence. Whatever your role, name the decline for what it is, a normal part of ageing.
blocks.sourceNote: Liu 2007 · Blackman 2002 · 21 U.S.C. 333(e) · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 14
